Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 10:54: Let us come to explain, in a chapter of its own, how great is the virtue of one who guards his mouth and tongue, and how great the blemish - although we have already explained some in this chapter, in the next chapter we shall add teaching, with God's help. And we have divided the matter into a chapter of its own, in order to give the reader room between one chapter and the next.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:1: It is written, "who is the man who desires life, who loves days to see good? Guard your tongue from evil," and so on (Psalms 34:13) - our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Avodah Zarah 19a, at the end): Rabbi Alexandri would proclaim, who wants life, who wants life? The whole world gathered and came to him. They said to him, give us life. He said to them, "who is the man who desires life," and so on, "guard your tongue," and so on, "turn from evil and do good." Perhaps a person will say, I have guarded my tongue from evil and my lips from speaking deceit, [so now] I shall indulge in sleep [idleness] - therefore Scripture says, "turn from evil and do good" - and "good" refers only to Torah, as it is said (Proverbs 4:2), "for I have given you good teaching; do not forsake My Torah" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:2: And this story is brought in the Midrash (Vayikra Rabbah 16:2) in another manner, and my teacher, peace be upon him, wrote that what it says, that he understood the verse only through that peddler, is because the verse is doubled, saying "who is the man who desires life" and then saying "who loves days to see good" - and it is resolved through the peddler proclaiming, who wants life? - for the whole world came to him - and if for the life of this world a person pursues to obtain a remedy by which he shall live, all the more so is it fitting that he pursue the life of the World to Come. And the days, which should be his "lovers" for the repair of his soul, it is fitting that he not sin in them through his tongue, in a manner that they not turn against him into enemies and accusers - and this is "loves days," that the days themselves become his lovers, for his good in the World to Come.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:3: And in the Zohar (Parashat Shemini, page 41a) this verse is explained, in these words: Rabbi Abba opened and said, "who is the man who desires life," and so on, "guard your tongue from evil," and so on, and it is written (Proverbs 21:23), "he who guards his mouth and his tongue," and so on. "Who is the man who desires life" - what is "life"? Rather, this is the life called the World to Come, and life dwells there - and therefore we have learned, "it is a tree of life" - a tree from that life, a tree planted in that life - and therefore it is written, "who is the man who desires life." "Who loves days to see good" - what are "days"? Rather, this is the Name of the holy King, which is bound to those supernal days called "the days of the heavens upon the earth" - "the days of the heavens," certainly, "upon the earth," certainly. Whoever wants the supernal life, to have a portion in them, and whoever wants the days, to cleave to them and love them, let him guard his mouth from everything, guard his mouth from food and drink that defiles the soul, and distance himself from those [things opposed to] that life and those days; let him guard his mouth from evil words, so as not to be defiled by them, and distance himself from them and have no portion in them. Come and see, mouth and tongue - another, supernal place is likewise called this - and therefore one should not blemish his mouth and his tongue, and all the more so not defile his own soul and body, because he is defiled in the other world - and this has been established.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:4: And what appears to us in explaining the verse, by the plain meaning, in saying "who is the man" - in the Zohar (Parashat Terumah, end of page 128a) it explains that whoever overcomes his inclination is called "ish" [a man] - and the reason he is called "man" who guards his tongue from evil is because the sin of the tongue is constant, and one who overcomes his inclination and does not speak at the time his inclination entices him to speak deserves to be called "man" - unlike other transgressions, where, even though he may overcome it once, it is not constant and does not raise him so much that he be called "man," as does one who guards his tongue.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:5: And it intends to tell us the great virtue a person attains by properly guarding the tongue. The first is the cause of cleaving to his God, as explained, that these are the essence of life, and concerning this the righteous one is called "living" - "and Benaiah son of Jehoiada, son of a living man" (2 Samuel 23:20), and likewise "and the living shall lay it to his heart" (Ecclesiastes 7:2) - and as the poet said, "in my distance from You is my death in my life, but if I cleave to You, my life is in my death." And what follows from his desiring life is that he loves the days, for the days are supernal illuminations drawn down below for the repair of the soul, and the hidden treasure for the righteous is hidden and concealed within the days, and whoever refines himself merits to see his world in his lifetime, as they said in Berachot (17a), "you shall see your world in your lifetime" - and this is "to see good," meaning to see his world in his lifetime - and only one who properly guards his tongue attains this virtue, and this is what it says there in the teaching, "your mouth shall speak wisdom, and your tongue shall silence songs" - and everything mentioned in the teaching is all preparation for what is mentioned at the beginning of the teaching, "you shall see your world in your lifetime, and your hope for generation after generation."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:6: And it says, "guard your tongue from evil" - agreed upon in the words of Rashbi, peace be upon him, in the Zohar (Parashat Bereshit, beginning of page 57), that the word "ra" [evil] is applied to one who emits seed in vain, and he bases the matter on the verse (Genesis 38:7), "and Er, Judah's firstborn, was evil [ra] in the eyes of the LORD" - meaning that he would emit seed in vain - and this is his wording, in brief, on this matter: Rabbi Yosi said, is "ra" not "rasha" [wicked]? He said to him, no - a "rasha" is even one who raises his hand against his fellow, even though he does nothing to him, is called "rasha," as it is written (Exodus 2:13), "and he said to the wicked one [rasha], why do you strike your fellow" - it does not say "you struck," but "you strike" [future/ongoing] - but "ra" is called only one who corrupts his way and defiles himself and defiles the land - to this point, relevant here. Behold, it is explicit that he speaks in a negative formulation, "ra" is called only [such], and so on.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:7: Now, along these lines it must be explained concerning the tongue - and the matter is that after it was explained that there are two covenants corresponding exactly to each other, the covenant of the tongue and the covenant of the flesh (end of Sefer Yetzirah, chapter 1, mishnah 2) - just as, with the covenant of the flesh, one who emits seed in vain is called "ra," so with the covenant of the tongue, one who emits a word in vain is like one who emits seed in vain, and therefore it says "guard your tongue from evil," so that you not be called "ra," who is the one who emits [in vain], as explained.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:8: And it says "netzor" [guard, a stronger word] and not "shemor" [guard, ordinary] or the like, to indicate great guarding, a fence and a wall within a wall, as the word "netzor" indicates - and so Radak explains in Sefer HaShorashim, that "netzor" is from the root of "matzor" [siege/fortification], along the lines of (Deuteronomy 20:20), "and you shall build a siege-wall against the city" - and it is the most excellent guarding.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:9: And so, in the word "netzor leshonecha" [guard your tongue], it does not say "netzor ha-lashon mera" [guard the tongue from evil], but "leshonecha" [your tongue] - meaning that you should see with the eye of the intellect that your tongue is surrounded by two walls, as they explained, of blessed memory (Arachin 15b), on the verse (Psalms 120:3), "what shall be given to you, and what more shall be done to you, you deceitful tongue" - the Holy One, blessed be He, said to the tongue: all of a person's limbs are upright and you are laid flat; all of a person's limbs are on the outside and you are on the inside; and not only that, but I have surrounded you with two walls, one of bone and one of flesh - "what shall be given to you," and so on - to this point. And this is the matter of "netzor" [guard], alluding to a hidden and concealed place, to indicate the siege-fortification of the two walls it has - and therefore the Creator concealed it with these concealments of the walls, which He did not do for the other limbs - and this is certainly because of its virtue, and it is like the parable of a person who stores his precious possession in a treasury within a treasury.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:10: And to explain the matter, why one who emits seed in vain and one who emits a word in vain are both called "ra," the reason is what we explained, that the tongue is in the place of life, as explained above concerning "who is the man who desires life" - and just as the seed is a physical vitality in a person, being from the light of his eyes, and so on (Rambam, Hilchot De'ot, chapter 4, halachah 19), and it begets physically, as is known, and one who emits it in vain is called "ra" because of the secret and allusion above within it - so the matter of the tongue, which is the fortification of the secret of the spiritual vitality clothed in the vessel of the tongue, begets above in spiritual holiness, and it is not fitting for it to be emitted in vain - and this is the virtue of a rabbi who never engaged in idle talk all his days.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:11: And although we said that "ra" is said of speech in vain, nevertheless anything blemished, that indicates an external force, is also called "ra" - and the proof is slander, which is harmful - and although some benefit might result from saying it, nevertheless it is called "ra" in itself, since the external force has a share in it - and the general rule of "guard your tongue" is: from any speech in which the external force, called "ra," has a share.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:12: And it says "leshonecha" [your tongue] and "sefatecha" [your lips] in the second-person form, to indicate what they said, of blessed memory, in Bereshit Rabbah (67:3), that the mouth is in a person's own domain - that if he wishes he speaks Torah and good, and if he wishes he speaks evil - and this is "leshonecha" and "sefatecha," which are in your own domain. In these words: Rabbi Levi said, six things serve a person, three in his domain and three not in his domain. The ear, the nose, and the eye are not in his domain - he sees what he does not wish, hears what he does not wish, smells what he does not wish. The mouth, the hand, and the foot are in his domain - if he wishes he labors in Torah, if he wishes he curses, if he wishes he does not curse. The hand - if he wishes he abounds in commandments, if he wishes he steals and kills. The foot - if he wishes he goes to synagogues and study halls, if he wishes he goes to theaters and circuses. At a time a person is meritorious, the Holy One, blessed be He, makes those in his domain not in his domain - the mouth: "and he shall also be blessed" (Genesis 27:33); the hand: "and his hand dried up" (1 Kings 13:4); the foot: "my son, do not walk in the way with them," and so on (Proverbs 1:15) - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:13: And it is written in Sefer Menorat HaMaor of Rabbi Yisrael, peace be upon him, that there are seven openings in the head, corresponding to the seven branches of the Menorah, and the mouth corresponds to the middle branch, which is holy - and therefore one must sanctify his mouth and tongue on the Sabbath day, which is the seventh and holy, for all sevenths are holy.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:14: And in the Tikkunim (page 137a): "the Torah of truth was in his mouth" (Malachi 2:6) - this is the Sanctuary, and concerning it is said (Psalms 51:17), "O Lord, open my lips" - within it is the Holy of Holies, and this is the heart - to this point. And reason dictates that speech be sanctified, since it emerges from the Holy of Holies, which is the heart, to the Sanctuary, which is the mouth. And further you shall find that the word "kadosh" [holy], spelled out in full with the reckoning of its four letters, totals the numerical value of "dibbur" [speech], spelled out in full.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:15: Further, it means "guard your tongue from evil" - that whoever blemishes his mouth with vulgar words and the like, they defile him and bring him to emit seed in vain, teaching him that he is "ra" - and as explained in the Zohar (Introduction, page 8a), on the verse (Ecclesiastes 5:5), "do not let your mouth cause your flesh to sin," in these words: Rav Hamnuna Sabba said, "do not let your mouth cause your flesh to sin" - that a person should not give his mouth to come to an evil lustful thought, and cause that holy flesh, sealed with the holy covenant, to sin - for if he does so, they lead him to Gehinnom, and the one appointed over Gehinnom, called Dumah, and how many myriads of destroying angels with him, stands at the gate of Gehinnom - and whoever guards the holy covenant in this world, he has no permission to approach him - to this point. And my teacher, peace be upon him, was precise in saying "that a person should not give his mouth to come," and so on - the intent being to be precise about the wording of the verse, which says "do not let your mouth cause your flesh to sin," and so on - for the intent is not to warn us merely not to sin with the tongue, for if so it should have said "do not sin with your mouth" - rather, even words that contain no vulgarity of the mouth, but would lead to lustful thought, are forbidden - such as speaking with one's wife about matters of intercourse, which would lead to lustful thought and cause his flesh, which is the holy covenant, to sin, by emitting seed in vain.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:16: And it is found from this that guarding the covenant depends on guarding the tongue, because they are two exactly corresponding covenants, as explained - and therefore Scripture puts guarding the tongue first, because it is the essential thing and includes the two hundred [i.e., is worth double] - for if he guards the tongue, the covenant is guarded of itself; but if he is not careful in guarding the tongue, even though he is careful in guarding the covenant, even the guarding of the covenant does not avail him - and the reason is explained in what we have said.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:17: And so it is also explained in Parashat Noach and in Parashat Acharei Mot, that whoever blemishes with his tongue is defiled, and is found to be called "ra" - at the end of Parashat Noach (page 76a) he says, in these words: Rabbi Yosi opened and said (Deuteronomy 23:15), "for the LORD your God walks in the midst of your camp, to deliver you and to give your enemies before you; therefore your camp shall be holy, that He see no unseemly thing [ervat davar] among you, and turn away from you" - "for the LORD your God walks [mit'halech]" - it should say "mehalech" [simple form] - rather, as it is said (Genesis 3:8), "walking [mit'halech] in the garden in the cool of the day" - and this is the tree from which the first man ate - "mit'halech" is feminine, "mehalech" is masculine - and this is what goes before Israel when they went in the wilderness, as it is written (Exodus 13:21), "and the LORD went before them by day," and so on - it is what goes before a person when he walks on a road, as it is written (Psalms 85:14), "righteousness shall go before Him, and shall set his footsteps on the way" - and this is what goes before a person at the time he is meritorious. And why? "To deliver you and to give your enemies" - to save a person on the road and so that another [power] not rule over him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:18: And therefore a person must guard himself from his sins and purify himself - what is purification? "Therefore your camp shall be holy" - what is "holy" [kadosh, singular]? It should say "holy" [kedoshim, plural] - rather, "your camp shall be holy" refers to the limbs of the body, with which the body is joined and repaired, and therefore "your camp shall be holy." "That He see no unseemly thing [ervat davar] among you" - what is "ervat davar"? This is the nakedness of forbidden relations, for this is a matter the Holy One, blessed be He, despises more than anything. Since it says "that He see no ervah among you," why "davar" [thing/word]? Rather, these wicked ones of the world, who defile and befoul themselves with their own word [davar] that emerges from their mouths - this is "ervat davar" - and why so much? Because He goes before you, and if you act thus, immediately "and turn away from you" - so that He not go with you and turn away from you - to this point. And so in Vayikra Rabbah (Parashat Kedoshim 24:7): "that He see no unseemly thing [ervat davar] among you" - the nakedness of speech [ervat dibbur] - Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachman said, this is vulgar speech - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:19: And in the Zohar (Parashat Acharei Mot, page 75b) it says: we have learned, there are two hundred forty-eight limbs in the body, and all of them are defiled when it is defiled, meaning that it is [made ready] to be defiled - and therefore, "your camp shall be holy" - what is "your camp"? These are the limbs of the body. "That He see no ervat davar among you" - what is "ervat davar"? The nakedness of this "davar" - an allusion, as we have established, and so on - to this point. And the rest of the teaching we copied in the Gate of Fear, chapter 5 - see there.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:20: And when we combine the two teachings, our intent emerges clearly explained - that according to all explanations, "your camp shall be holy" refers to the two hundred forty-eight limbs, and therefore "your camp" is mentioned in the plural form, to indicate the two hundred forty-eight limbs. And what is said in Parashat Noach, that "ervat davar" is the nakedness of speech, and what is said in Parashat Acharei Mot, that "ervat davar" is the Shechinah, are all one - for whoever blemishes the nakedness of speech blemishes her, since speech is from her - and this is what the teaching (in Parashat Noach) began with, saying "for YHVH your God walks [feminine form]" - this is the female.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:21: And of necessity we must say, according to our approach, that "your camp shall be holy," referring to the two hundred forty-eight, [means] that "walks in the midst of your camp" also refers to the camp of the body - for the totality of the two hundred forty-eight is one camp in which the soul rests, and the soul, since it comes from the Atzilut of the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Shechinah, and it walks within the body - the soul has no life to produce the power of speech except according to how the Shechinah bestows it, for the soul is a thread drawn from above from these two measures, as it says (Deuteronomy 32:9), "for the LORD's portion is His people" - and it is impossible to separate the portion from its root. It follows that since the soul is below, that "YHVH your God" is literally "walks in the midst of your camp," and this is "YHVH your God" - the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Shechinah, from whom is the emanation of the soul, and they are voice and speech.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:22: And the reason it says "mit'halech" [feminine] and not "mehalech" [masculine] is because the essential thing in man is speech, and voice is secondary to it, therefore it says "mit'halech" [feminine, matching speech/the Shechinah]. And likewise, the place of the soul's gestation is within her, and she is the mother who bears it, and she raises the children - therefore she is the essential thing in this matter. And therefore it says, "that He see no ervat davar among you" - meaning, the Shechinah, who walks within you, along the lines explained, that she is the soul, and so on, should not see [him make] her power go out in vain, to a place of nakedness, namely speech. And therefore it says that "ervat dibbur" [nakedness of speech] is more despised than anything, because it is a blemish in the Shechinah and in the soul, though only in a spiritual aspect - for speech is more spiritual than deed, as explained above concerning "who is the man who desires life."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:23: And it says "your camp shall be holy" - that the two hundred forty-eight limbs be on the side of holiness and not be defiled - as it says in Parashat Acharei Mot, "two hundred forty-eight limbs in the body, and all of them are defiled" - and there is no sin that defiles all two hundred forty-eight limbs like the sin of seminal emission, for the seed emerges from all his two hundred forty-eight limbs, and all of them are defiled by the spirit of impurity from Lilith resting upon him. And through this the matter "that He see no ervat davar among you" is precisely understood - meaning, He shall not see, in your body, a nakedness of speech - for when the Shechinah is blemished, which you have blemished, the blemish in her shows in your body, and the nakedness, which is Lilith, "ervat davar," rests upon you, and then the Shechinah withdraws from you, and this is "and turn away from you," for "evil shall not sojourn with You" (Psalms 5:5).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:24: And there is proof for this explanation in Vayikra Rabbah, Parashat Zavim (18:4): where were Israel obligated in flux [zivah] and leprosy? Rav Huna in the name of Rabbi Hoshaya said, because they would slander their leaders, saying, this family of so-and-so is not free of leprosy - to teach you that plagues come only because of slander. Rabbi Tanchuma said, because they would slander the Ark, saying, this Ark kills its bearers - and plagues come only because of slander - therefore Israel became obligated in flux and leprosy - to this point. Behold, it is explicit that flux came to them through the blemish of slander. And flux blemishes the covenant, and my teacher, peace be upon him, explained that "zav" [flux] totals nine, for its blemish is in the Righteous One [Yesod], the ninth attribute - and likewise concerning seminal emission, whose blemish is in the covenant, as we shall elaborate in its place - its cause shall be the blemish of the tongue, through slander and the other things that blemish the tongue.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:25: And so it is explained in Parashat Metzora (page 53a), whose wording we shall copy below: Rabbi Chiya said, whoever utters slander, all his limbs become defiled, and so on - and this is along the lines of "two hundred forty-eight limbs in the body, and all of them are defiled," as explained.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:26: Further, it is possible to explain "that He see no ervat davar among you" as explained in the Zohar (Parashat Naso, page 121b), close to the previous approach, in these words: come and see, at the time people sleep and taste the taste of death, and the soul ascends above, it stands in the place it stands, and is examined concerning its deeds performed that whole day, and they write it on a note - why? Because the soul ascends above and testifies concerning a person's deeds and concerning every single word emerging from his mouth, because that word a person utters from his mouth ascends and splits the firmaments, and stands in the place it stands, until night enters and the soul ascends and takes hold of that word and brings it before the King - this is what is written (Micah 7:5), "guard the doors of your mouth from her who lies in your bosom" - and then that word and that sin are marked upon the person, and therefore (Psalms 32:2), "happy is the man against whom the LORD counts no iniquity" - when? When there is no deceit in his spirit - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:27: Behold, it says "that word and that sin are marked upon the person," and it is explained by what is known, that some sins are marked and written on the skin of the flesh of the face, and some on the forehead, and some are engraved on his bones, as they explained, of blessed memory - and this is "marked upon the person" - literally upon him is marked the sin of that speech.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:28: And even though he performed no deed, nevertheless speech is more severe than deed, as explained in the Mishnah (Arachin, chapter 3, mishnah 5) - it is found that one who says with his mouth is [more culpable] than one who performs a deed, for we find that the decree against our forefathers in the wilderness was not sealed except because of slander, as it is said (Numbers 14:22), "and have tested Me [with their words]." And we learn from this, that if he thought in his mind to commit a transgression and decided in his mind to do it, and uttered that decision with his lips, it is accounted before Him, blessed be He, as though he did it, for speech is accounted like a deed, as they said in the Mishnah. And they said, of blessed memory (Kiddushin 40a), only that a person who thought to commit a transgression and did not commit it, it is not accounted to him, is when he did not speak - and this is (Psalms 66:18), "if I had regarded iniquity in my heart, the LORD would not have heard" - but if I spoke with my lips, the LORD would hear. And so it is explained in the Zohar (Parashat Emor, page 105a) concerning speech on the Sabbath, that speech is forbidden because the voice immediately ascends above, but lustful thought is permitted. And so Rashbi, peace be upon him, explained in the Idra of Ha'azinu (page 294a), in the repair of the ears - see there. And so it is explained in the previous chapter on the verse "do not be rash with your mouth," and so on - see there.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:29: And through this "that He see no ervat davar among you" is understood - meaning that the nakedness of that speech is imprinted and marked in his body, and this is "bach" [in you] - literally, in your body it is marked - and once the body is blemished by transgression, it is blemished, and the Shechinah withdraws from it - and this is "and turn away from you," for "whoever has a blemish shall not approach" (Leviticus 21:18).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:30: Further, it is possible to explain "that He see no [unseemly thing] among you" [bach] along the lines explained in the Zohar (Zohar Chadash, Shir HaShirim, page 68a) concerning "let us be glad and rejoice in you [bach]" (Song of Songs 1:4), that "bach" is the twenty-two letters, and "bach" is Tiferet. And it is known that the twenty-two letters of the Torah are marked in a person's mouth, as explained above concerning "do not be rash with your mouth," which are Alef-Chet-Heh-Ayin in the throat, and so on - and it means, "He shall not see 'bach'" - He shall not see the Torah, which is fixed in your mouth in the twenty-two letters, [if] you utter its letters for speech of nakedness - for it is found that you blemish the five supernal points of articulation, which are the source of the twenty-two letters. And when he considers where the supernal allusion of each and every point of articulation is, he shall see how great is the blemish of the tongue - and the allusion is seen in a person's mouth, in that he has thirty-two teeth, corresponding to the thirty-two paths of Chokhmah, which are the thirty-two [mentions of] "Elohim" in the account of creation - and this is one of the points of articulation, Zayin-Tzadi-Samech-Resh-Shin, in the teeth, and likewise the other points of articulation, Alef-Chet-Heh-Ayin in the throat - the throat being more internal, the blemish there is greater, and likewise for the other points of articulation - it follows that the blemish is in all of them together. And therefore it says, "that He see no 'bach'" - meaning the twenty-two letters that are in the five points of articulation - "ervat davar," that a blemish of the nakedness of speech be found in them. And this is also the secret of Tiferet, called "bach," which comprises the twenty-two letters of the Torah - He shall see no "ervat davar," which is His Shechinah - for when He sees the Shechinah blemished, He withdraws, and this is "and turn away from you," from which it follows that mercy withdraws from him, along the lines explained in the Gate of Fear, chapter 5.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:31: Now, from all the explanations set forth on this verse, we can understand what the Tanna said (Avot, chapter 1, mishnah 17), "all my days I grew up among the Sages, and I found nothing," and so on. And the explanation of "all my days I grew up" is that a person, according to the place he grows up in, learns qualities, whether for good or the opposite - and therefore he says that he grew up among the Sages, and what he learned from them is that he found nothing better than silence - and among the Sages this quality must necessarily be found, for they said (Avot, chapter 5, mishnah 7), "seven things characterize a sage," and so on: "a sage does not speak in the presence of one greater than him in wisdom, and does not interrupt his fellow's words" - and the root of all the other qualities mentioned concerning a sage is silence.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:32: "I have found nothing better for the body than silence" - what is the matter of "the body"? Let it say, "I have found nothing better than silence"? Rather, the matter, according to our explanation, that the two hundred forty-eight limbs are defiled - it means, I have found no better purity for the body than silence - and support for this explanation I found in the words of our Rabbis, of blessed memory (Vayikra Rabbah 16:5), which we copied in chapter 13, on "cause your flesh to sin" - do not give permission to one of your limbs to cause all your limbs to sin. Or, according to the explanation that the blemish is marked in his body - if he does not sin with his mouth and stays silent, certainly that sin will not be marked in his body, and likewise mercy will not withdraw from him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:33: Or it is possible to say, "I have found nothing for the body" - meaning, for the affairs of the body, silence is good, but for words of Torah one must speak, along the lines of "silence of righteousness" explained above. Further, it means "for the body," along the lines explained in the Midrash concerning (Proverbs 18:21), "death and life are in the hand of the tongue" - the parable of the lion cub they said in the Midrash (Yalkut Tehillim, remez 721).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:34: Further, I found in Tanna DeVei Eliyahu, that a certain man, after he passed away, was found by the gravediggers in his grave still alive, for the worm had not ruled over him, and Rav Nachman asked him what merit brought him this - and he answered that he had no envy and did not incline his ear to hear idle words - and we copied this teaching in the Gate of Humility, chapter 3, and at the end of the teaching it says, and this one, who had nothing but the reward of silence alone, and so on.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:35: And in Sefer Menorat HaMaor of Rabbi Yisrael, peace be upon him, another explanation is given, in these words: I have found no remedy for the body but silence, for whoever multiplies words is not saved from sin, and shall be afflicted with leprosy in his body. And in light of what Rashbi, peace be upon him, explained (Zohar, Parashat Mishpatim, page 122a), in these words: we have learned, it is written (Psalms 34:14), "guard your tongue from evil [mera]" - what is "mera"? Because of slander, illnesses [mar'in] descend to the world - to this point - we shall explain, "I have found nothing for the body" that would be saved from evil illnesses - not specifically leprosy, as he explains, but all illnesses - "but silence," through which he is saved - and this is a great virtue of silence.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:36: And in the Midrash (Vayikra Rabbah, Parashat Metzora 16:5): Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said, a word is worth a sela, silence two - for we have learned, his son Shimon says, all my days I grew up among the Sages and found nothing better for the body than silence - to this point. And through this explanation, two precise points that need examining in the Mishnah are resolved: the first, why it enters into a negative formulation; the second, the word "better" [tov] - for one does not say "this is better than that" unless they are in the same category and of equal standing, and then one says "this is better than that." And through this everything is resolved - for it comes to teach us that a word is worth a sela, silence worth two - and this is what it says, "I have found nothing for the body better than silence" - that even though speech is worth a sela, silence is better than it and worth two - and it does not, by this, exclude silence from idle talk, slander, and the like, for in these speech is not good at all, so that we could say silence is better than speech - and there is no equivalence in selas for them, for on the contrary, they are blemishing.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:37: And the pious one, of blessed memory, wrote in his commentary on this Mishnah, in these words: and one who refrains from speaking where he has need to speak indicates three things about his soul: the first, that he is knowledgeable, since he is not rash to speak, meaning, "an empty jug clatters" [i.e., he is not empty]; the second, that his intellect overpowers his materiality and therefore he restrains his words; the third, that he is understanding and his eyes are in his head, to see the harm fitting to come from his words - and this is what Solomon said (Proverbs 17:27), "he who restrains his words is knowledgeable; a man of understanding has a cool spirit" - in saying "restrains," it teaches that he has need to speak and even so restrains himself, for this is the common usage of the term - "and I too withheld [va'echsoch]" (Genesis 20:6), "he has withheld [lo chasach] nothing from me" (ibid. 39:9) - and so Rabbi Yosef ibn Shoshan, of blessed memory, wrote, and he is described with three descriptions: "knowledgeable," "of cool spirit," "a man of understanding" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:38: And it appears to me that these three descriptions correspond to Chokhmah, Binah, Da'at, and it begins with Da'at, which is the essence of the tongue, and afterward "yekar ru'ach" [cool/precious spirit], which is the honor of the heart from Chokhmah, from where the spirit of life flows, [then] "a man of understanding" corresponding to Binah - and because he holds the place of life, as explained concerning "who is the man who desires life," it is fitting that he be described by these three.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 11:39: And the Tanna connected to this, saying, "not the exposition is the essential thing, but the deed." It is possible to connect his words in two ways: the first, that he comes to tell us that having taught us this good quality, that he found nothing better for the body than silence, his students afterward, when they cite this quality, should not intend only to study it and not practice it, so that it be found "attractive in teaching but not attractive in practice," but rather that they practice and acquire the quality of silence - and the same applies to all matters a person is called to practice, that not the exposition is the essential thing. And the reason he taught us this matter concerning the tongue is that a person's acquisition of this quality requires great effort, because of the habit of the tongue and its swiftness to speak good and evil - and whoever fulfills this quality shall have a key to acquiring all the other good qualities that exist, and it is well for him to study and practice, for once he has grasped his root and guarded it properly, all the branches shall endure.
